latin: Altera stēlla ā glōriōsō quōdam incolēbatur. Quī simul ac<sup>1</sup> rēgulum cōnspexit, procul exclāmāvit: «Ecce hūc<sup>2</sup> venit quī mē admīrātur»...
Tertia ā pōtātōre incolēbatur: Rēgulus. — Cūr pōtās?
In cēterīs stēllīs, vīsitāvit Rēgulus negōtiātōrem quemdam quī dīvitiās<sup>4</sup> suās sine fīne computābat,...
lychnōrum pūblicōrum cūrātōrem<sup>5</sup> quī immānī<sup>6</sup> mūnere sē fungī exīstimābat, nam stēlla ejus singulīs minūtīs circumagēbātur,...
geographum dēnique quī librōs ingentēs scrībēbat:
Geographus. — At tū ē locīs remōtīs vēnīs. Ignōta explōrās. Jam mihi stēllam tuam dēscrībe!
Reg. — Domī meae omnia perparva sunt. Mihi sunt trēs ignivomī<sup>7</sup> montēs, quōrum duo etiamnunc ārdeant, ūnus exstīnctus sit... mihi etiam flōs est...
Gēō. — Dē flōribus mentiōnem facere nōn solēmus in tractātibus nostrīs.
Reg. — Quidnī? Sunt fōrmōsissimae rērum omnium<sup>8</sup>.
Reg. — Quae mē hortārīs ut vīsam<sup>10</sup>?
Gēō. — Terram stēllam. Nam bene audit. Abiit* rēgulus, sēcum dē flōre suō cōgitāns.

english: The second star was inhabited by a vain man. As soon as he saw the little prince, he cried out from afar: «Here [comes an admirer] (here comes he who admires me)»...
The third was inhabited by a drinker: The little prince. — Why do you drink?
The drinker. — [To forget] (so that I may forget).
Prince. — [To forget what] (of what thing that you forget)?
Drinker. — To forget that I am ashamed.
Prince. — [What] are you ashamed of?
Drinker. — I am ashamed of drinking...
On the other stars, the little prince visited a businessman who counted his riches without stopping,...
a lamplighter [of public] lamps who considered that he had a terrible job, for his star made [a] turn each minute (singular)...
a geographer finally, who wrote very large books:
The geographer. — So, you come from [far away] (remote places). You explore unknown [regions]. [Now describe] your planet [to me] (already described)!
Prince. — At my place everything [is] very small. I have three volcanoes, two of which are (subj.) still [active] (burning) and one is (subj.) extinct... I also have a flower...
Geo. — We are not in the habit of mentioning flowers in our treatises.
Prince. — Why not? They are the most beautiful of all things.
Geo. — Because flowers are ephemeral...
Prince. — What do you advise me to visit?
Geo. — The planet Earth. [It has a good reputation] (for it hears well). The little prince went away, thinking of his flower.

footnotes: Simul, adv., at the same time; simul ac, simul atque, as soon as.
Huc, like istuc and illuc, designates the place where one is going: huc venis, you come where I am; istuc venit, he goes where you are; etc.
Me pudet, impersonal verb. Shame is said pudor, -oris, m.
Divitiae, -arum, f. pl., riches; dives, -itis, adj., rich.
Curator, from curare, to take care. Likewise you will have curator viarum, the one who maintains the roads. — Lychnus, -i, m., the lamp.

Vulcanus, -i, m., Vulcan; the god of fire gave his name to volcanoes. But, in antiquity, this name was not used as a common noun; that is why we find instead of vulcani a periphrasis: mountains which spit fire (ignivomus, -a, -um; from ignis and from vomo, -is, -ere, -ui, -itum, to vomit).

Formosissimae rerum: the complement of the superlative is either in the genitive, as here, or preceded by inter. It is then put in the accusative: formosissimus inter flores, the most beautiful among the flowers. N.B. — Res is feminine and flos masculine.

Evanesco, -is, -ere, evanui, v.i., to vanish, to disappear, whence the adjective evanidus. Caducus, -a, -um, caducous, perishable (from cadere, to fall) would have been more precise, but would have represented less well the intention of the author.

Hortari, deponent verb of the 1st conjugation, to exhort. It is construed with ad + acc. if its complement is an indirect object (e.g. te hortor ad patientiam, I exhort you to patience), or with ut and the subjunctive as in P. 16. Viso, -is, -ere, -i, visum, to look at attentively (a sense slightly different from that of videre).
comments: Perhaps you think, and quite rightly, that we have mutilated the beautiful story of the little prince. That is because the aim we are pursuing is above all to teach you a language, by giving you examples as varied as possible, of words and Latin expressions, with the sole connection necessary to sustain your attention. So do not be surprised to find cuts and modifications which often take us far from the original text.

If you want, as we hope, to know more about it, you can from now on begin to draw directly from the sources, which you will find elsewhere in the list in the BIBLIOGRAPHICAL INDEX which is found at the very end of the book.

Chicago, -inis, f., is declined like Carthago, -inis, Carthage. One also says Chicagia, -ae, f. — Camberium, -ii, n., Chambéry, capital of Savoy. — Gratianopolis (cf. L. 31, N. 4) makes its acc. in im.
You will not have failed to notice that this exercise bore exclusively on complements of place. If you like, we will put some order into it during our next revision.

english: Hey there! Stephen! Where are you? I hear you singing, but I can't see where you are.
I'm at the house; I'm in the loft where we keep the grain (wheat).
In the new house, there is no loft.
I'm coming down from the loft.
Get out of the house!
I don't want to leave the old house.
I want to leave Paris.
Let's go to the loft.
You don't want to go to the house?
They prefer to go to Chicago.
We're not going to the city of New York.
We're not going to New York, the famous city.
We are heading for Grenoble by the valley of the Isère.
We are heading for Chambéry by the Aemilian Way.
Aren't you coming from Milan?
Yes, we passed through Aosta.
